title: “All Things Are Possible” — The Verse We Quote, the Context We Ignore, and the Grace That Changes Everything
paragraphs:
“All Things Are Possible” — The Verse We Quote, the Context We Ignore, and the Grace That Changes Everything
The Hidden Meaning Behind Jesus’ Most Misunderstood Promise—and Why It Might Be the Hope Your Heart Has Been Desperate to Find
There are verses people love to put on coffee mugs, wall frames, social media graphics, graduation cards, gym shirts, and motivational posters.
Few are quoted more often than these words:
“With God all things are possible.” — Matthew 19:26
People quote it when chasing dreams.
They quote it when starting businesses.
They quote it when pursuing success.
They quote it before exams, competitions, interviews, and impossible goals.
Yet one of the greatest ironies in modern Christianity is that many people celebrate this verse while completely missing the shocking conversation that produced it.
Because Jesus was not talking about becoming rich.
He was not talking about achieving personal ambitions.
He was not talking about winning earthly success.
He was talking about something infinitely more impossible.
He was talking about salvation.
He was talking about a scandalous grace so powerful that no human effort could ever produce it.
He was talking about the miracle of God saving people who cannot save themselves.
And when we understand the deeper meaning of “all things are possible,” the Gospel becomes even more beautiful than we imagined.
The story begins with a man who looked successful in every measurable way.
Matthew 19 introduces what many call the Rich Young Ruler.
He was moral.
Religious.
Respected.
Disciplined.
Successful.
The kind of person most churches would probably admire.
The kind of person society would celebrate.
The kind of person many believers secretly wish they could be.
Yet beneath the polished image was a heart still searching.
He approached Jesus and asked:
“Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life?” (Matthew 19:16)
Notice the assumption.
“What must I do?”
The question itself reveals the human condition.
We naturally believe eternal life can be earned.
We assume there must be a ladder.
A formula.
A spiritual achievement.
A score high enough for God to finally accept us.
But Jesus begins exposing the man's heart.
Eventually He tells him:
“If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” (Matthew 19:21)
The man walks away sorrowful.
Not because Jesus was cruel.
Not because wealth itself was evil.
But because his possessions possessed him.
His money revealed where his true worship lived.
Then Jesus says something that stunned everyone listening:
“It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” (Matthew 19:24)
The disciples were shocked.
In the ancient Jewish mindset, wealth was often viewed as evidence of God's blessing.
If someone as moral, disciplined, successful, and outwardly blessed as this man could not enter the Kingdom, then who could?
Their response carries genuine panic:
“Who then can be saved?” (Matthew 19:25)
Now we arrive at the famous verse.
The verse people print on posters.
The verse people memorize.
The verse many misunderstand.
Jesus looked at them and said:
“With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” (Matthew 19:26)
The Greek text reads:
Παρὰ ἀνθρώποις τοῦτο ἀδύνατόν ἐστιν, παρὰ δὲ Θεῷ πάντα δυνατά.
Transliterated:
Para anthrōpois touto adynaton estin, para de Theō panta dynata.
Literally:
“With humans this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”
Notice what Jesus actually says.
The impossible thing is not becoming wealthy.
The impossible thing is not achieving dreams.
The impossible thing is not accomplishing goals.
The impossible thing is salvation itself.
Human beings cannot rescue themselves.
No amount of morality can save us.
No amount of church attendance can save us.
No amount of religious performance can save us.
No amount of good works can save us.
The disciples asked:
“Who can be saved?”
Jesus answered:
“No one—unless God does it.”
That changes everything.
Because suddenly the Bible becomes a story not about human achievement but divine intervention.
Not about climbing up to God.
But about God coming down to us.
This truth echoes throughout Scripture.
The prophet Isaiah declared:
“All our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment.” (Isaiah 64:6)
The Hebrew phrase is startling:
כָּל־צִדְקֹתֵינוּ כְּבֶגֶד עִדִּים
Transliterated:
Kol-tsidqotenu keveged iddim.
Even our best efforts cannot erase sin.
Even our greatest accomplishments cannot produce righteousness.
The Apostle Paul reaches the same conclusion:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)
The Greek word for sin is:
ἁμαρτία (hamartia)
Meaning “to miss the mark.”
Humanity is not merely imperfect.
Humanity is incapable of achieving God's perfect standard.
That is why Jesus came.
The Gospel begins where human ability ends.
Many people spend years exhausting themselves trying to become worthy of God.
They hide struggles.
Hide addictions.
Hide failures.
Hide shame.
Hide wounds.
Hide secrets.
They become experts at looking holy while quietly falling apart inside.
Some reading this know exactly what that feels like.
You know what it is like to smile while carrying guilt.
You know what it is like to sit in church while fighting battles nobody knows.
You know what it is like to wonder whether God could ever truly forgive what happened.
You know what it is like to remember your worst moment and fear it defines your future.
Yet the Gospel repeatedly tells the story of people who should have been disqualified.
David committed adultery and murder.
Rahab was a prostitute.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted believers.
The Samaritan woman carried a scandalous past.
Yet God rewrote every story.
Not because they were strong enough.
Not because they deserved it.
Not because they finally achieved perfection.
But because grace stepped into the middle of their failure.
That is why our message has always been:
Because Scripture is not ultimately the story of good people finding God.
It is the story of a holy God rescuing broken people.
The deepest meaning of “all things are possible” is not that God helps us accomplish our plans.
It is that God accomplishes what we never could.
He saves sinners.
He transforms hearts.
He breaks chains.
He raises the spiritually dead.
He forgives the unforgivable.
He restores the seemingly ruined.
He rewrites stories that look beyond redemption.
The Aramaic-speaking followers of Jesus understood something we often forget.
The God who makes all things possible is not a cosmic vending machine fulfilling wishes.
He is the Redeemer.
The Deliverer.
The Savior.
The One who specializes in impossibilities that reveal His glory.
Perhaps the greatest impossibility in your life is not financial.
Not professional.
Not relational.
Perhaps the greatest impossibility is believing that God could still love you after everything you've done.
That is where grace enters.
The Cross is proof that God's answer to human impossibility is not condemnation but Christ.
At Calvary, Jesus carried what we could never carry.
Paid what we could never pay.
Accomplished what we could never accomplish.
The Gospel is not advice.
It is news.
Good news.
The news that Jesus succeeded where humanity failed.
The news that grace is greater than sin.
The news that redemption is stronger than shame.
The news that your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Because Jesus still rewrites stories.
Maybe that is why this verse continues to resonate across generations.
Deep down, every human being knows they need a miracle.
Not merely a better life.
A new life.
Not merely improvement.
Transformation.
Not merely inspiration.
Salvation.
And Jesus says the impossible becomes possible when God intervenes.
Sit with it.
Let it search you.
Let it remind you that your value is not found in your achievements, failures, status, reputation, wealth, or past.
It is found in the Savior who willingly went to the Cross for you.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
The greatest miracle was never that God could give you what you wanted.
The greatest miracle is that Jesus gave you what you could never earn.
